---
title: "Analytical workflow"
---

This page presents a step-by-step workflow for constructing a multimetabolite signature (MMS), covering all key steps from the raw data preparation to the downstream epidemiological applications. The framework is designed to be adaptable across studies.

I hope this offers a useful and inspiring starting point for developing your own MMS workflow! 🧪📊✨

# Data import and preprocessing {#data-import}

## Data structure {#data-structure}

For a supervised MMS approach, the minimum required variables are:

![](/images/data%20structure%20example.png){fig-align="center" fig-cap="Data structure example" width="57%"}

-   **subject identifiers**,

-   **metabolomics features**,

-   at least one **exposure variable**.

Additional elements could be included depending on the study design, such as:

-   multiple exposures for parallel signature construction,

-   covariates for adjustment or residualization,

-   metadata linking feature IDs to metabolite annotations,

-   downstream outcomes for later epidemiological analyses

For **example**, consider a substudy of 500 participants, each with a unique subject ID and measured metabolomics data. The metabolomics features could be used as predictors to construct an MMS for a specific exposure, such as the Alternative Healthy Eating Index (AHEI) dietary score. Additional variables, such as age, sex, and BMI, could be included as model covariates, or used in sensitivity analyses. A downstream health outcome, such as incident type 2 diabetes, could then be used in later epidemiological analyses to evaluate whether the MMS is associated with disease risk.

**Organise datasets for subsequent analyses**

There are several ways to organise datasets for downstream analyses. For example, all variables can be combined into a single dataset, with predictors, covariates, and exposures specified during analysis. Alternatively, the data can be split into separate subsets by type.

The key requirement is that, for the downstream analyses, the predictor matrix (e.g., metabolomics data) is clearly distinguished from exposures, covariates, and other participant-level metadata.

In the workflow example below, I chose to split the data into two datasets: one containing the feature columns used to build the signature, and another containing exposures, outcomes, covariates, and related metadata. I found this structure more convenient, and the helper functions are built with it in mind.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Variables organisation"
# Example: define metabolite feature columns
feature_columns <- colnames(dataset)[feature_start_col:ncol(dataset)]

# Create a dataset with features only
features_df <- dataset[, feature_columns, drop = FALSE]

# Convert feature dataset to model matrix
feature_matrix <- as.matrix(features_df)

# Example: define non-feature variables
exposure_columns <- c("exposure_1")               # replace with your exposure variable(s)
outcome_columns  <- c("outcome_1", "outcome_2")  # replace with your outcome variable(s)
covariate_columns <- c("age", "sex", "bmi")      # replace with your covariates
id_columns <- c("participant_id")                # optional: participant IDs or other metadata

# Create a dataset with participant-level metadata
metadata_df <- dataset[, c(id_columns, exposure_columns, outcome_columns, covariate_columns), drop = FALSE]
```
:::

## Exposure variables {#exposure-variables}

The target exposure can be a single variable or several related variables if multiple signatures are built in parallel.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Exposure variables"
# Example target exposures for parallel MMS construction
target_outcomes <- c(
  exposure_a = "exposure_a_residual",
  exposure_b = "exposure_b_residual",
  exposure_c = "exposure_c_residual",
  exposure_d = "exposure_d_residual"
)
```
:::

## Outcome definitions {#outcome-definitions}

If the MMS will later be related to disease, mortality, or another endpoint, it is helpful to define those downstream datasets early so the training and testing workflow is explicit.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Outcome definitions"
evaluation_ids <- evaluation_registry_df %>%
  dplyr::pull(participant_id)
```
:::

## Training and testing subsets {#training-and-testing-subsets}

At minimum, an MMS workflow requires both a **training** and a **testing datasets**. These can be obtained in two ways:

-   by using two separate datasets (one for model training and the other for external validation), or

-   by splitting a single dataset into training and testing subsets (e.g., random split).

In both situations, the training and testing dataset must contain the same variables and be similarly structured.

![](/images/train_test.png){fig-align="center" fig-cap="Training and testing dataset strategies" width="57%"}

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "User-defined training/test individuals"
#| 
  # Participants reserved for external or downstream evaluation
evaluation_ids <- external_registry_df %>%
  dplyr::pull(participant_id)

# Training population
train_data <- data %>%
  filter(!participant_id %in% evaluation_ids)

# Testing or external evaluation population
test_data <- data %>%
  filter(participant_id %in% evaluation_ids)

```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Random training/test splitting helper"

# Example helper-based split
split_dataset <- function(data, training_prop = 0.7, strata = NULL) {
  split_obj <- if (is.null(strata)) {
    rsample::initial_split(data, prop = training_prop)
  } else {
    rsample::initial_split(data, prop = training_prop, strata = {{ strata }})
  }

  list(
    split = split_obj,
    train_data = rsample::training(split_obj),
    test_data = rsample::testing(split_obj)
  )
}

# Example use
set.seed(123)

data_split <- split_dataset(
  data = dataset,
  training_prop = 0.7
)

train_data <- data_split$train_data
test_data  <- data_split$test_data
```
:::

::: {.callout-note .callout-strata-note collapse="true"}
## `strata`

This note refers to the optional `strata` argument inside `split_dataset()`.

Stratification helps keep the training and testing sets similar with respect to an important variable, usually the outcome or exposure grouping. This makes model training and evaluation more stable and more comparable. For example:

-   If your outcome is binary and rare, a purely random split might put too few cases in the test set.
-   If your target has strong class imbalance, stratification preserves roughly the same proportion in both subsets.

Use stratification when:\
- you have a categorical outcome like case/control\
- you have strong imbalance between groups\
- you want both train and test to represent the same population structure

You usually do not need it when:\
- the dataset is large and well balanced\
- the outcome is continuous and you are doing a simple random split.
:::

::: {.callout-note .callout-strata-note collapse="true"}
## `training_prop = 0.7`

This note refers to the optional `training_prop` argument inside `split_dataset()`.

This argument defines the proportion of individuals kept in the training dataset.

If you do not specify it, the default is `0.7`, meaning that 70% of individuals are assigned to the training dataset and the remaining 30% to the testing dataset.
:::

## Data wrangling {#data-wrangling}

The data needs to go through a series of steps prior to using it to train and test the MMS. These normally are:

-   missing value handling,

-   imputation,

-   transformation,

-   normalization / scaling,

-   batch correction (depending on the method),

-   possible feature selection,

One point to remember is to treat these steps independently in the training and testing data to never let test data influence the preprocessing steps.

### Missing value handling {#missing-value-handling}

Missing metabolite values should be addressed before model fitting, using a strategy aligned with the study design.

In a supervised MMS workflow:

-   **predictors** such as metabolite features can be imputed

-   **covariates** can often also be imputed, depending on the analysis plan

-   **target exposure** is usually **not imputed**. The target exposure it what the model is trying to learn from. If you impute it you may casually add noise or bias to the supervised signal, make interpretation harder and create a signature driven by assumptions from the imputation model rather than the observed data. Therefore, rows with missing target values should be removed.\

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Remove rows with missing target"

train_data <- train_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(.data[[target_col]]))

test_data <- test_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(.data[[target_col]]))

```
:::

### Imputation {#imputation}

Different variable groups often need different imputation rules. For example, metabolite features may use a low-value rule such as half-minimum, while numeric covariates may use the median and categorical covariates may use the mode.

The helper below keeps this flexible while staying simple: you use the same `impute()` function on both training and testing data, and for the test set you point `reference_data` to the already prepared training data so the imputation values are derived from the training set only.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Generic imputation helper"
impute <- function(data, cols, method = c("median", "mean", "mode", "halfmin"),
                   reference_data = data) {
  method <- match.arg(method)

  cols <- tidyselect::eval_select(rlang::expr(c({{ cols }})), data = data)
  cols <- names(cols)

  if (length(cols) == 0) {
    return(data)
  }

  get_mode <- function(x) {
    x_no_na <- x[!is.na(x)]
    if (length(x_no_na) == 0) return(NA)
    unique_values <- unique(x_no_na)
    unique_values[which.max(tabulate(match(x_no_na, unique_values)))]
  }

  values <- switch(
    method,
    median = sapply(reference_data[cols], function(x) median(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    mean = sapply(reference_data[cols], function(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    mode = sapply(reference_data[cols], get_mode),
    halfmin = sapply(reference_data[cols], function(x) {
      observed <- x[!is.na(x) & x > 0]
      if (length(observed) == 0) return(NA_real_)
      min(observed) / 2
    })
  )

  for (nm in cols) {
    data[[nm]][is.na(data[[nm]])] <- values[[nm]]
  }

  data
}
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Imputation in train and test data"
train_data <- train_data %>%
  impute(cols = all_of(feature_cols), method = "halfmin") %>%
  impute(cols = all_of(numeric_covariates), method = "median") %>%
  impute(cols = all_of(categorical_covariates), method = "mode")

test_data <- test_data %>%
  impute(cols = all_of(feature_cols), method = "halfmin", reference_data = train_data) %>%
  impute(cols = all_of(numeric_covariates), method = "median", reference_data = train_data) %>%
  impute(cols = all_of(categorical_covariates), method = "mode", reference_data = train_data)
```
:::

**Transformation**

In MMS development, transformation is used to improve the distributional properties of metabolite features before model training, for example by reducing skewness, stabilizing variance, and limiting the influence of extreme values. Log transformation is commonly used for positive-valued metabolomics data, but other approaches such as inverse normal or Box-Cox may be more appropriate depending on the data distribution and whether features include zero or negative values. When transformation parameters are estimated from the data, they should be defined using the training dataset and then applied unchanged to the testing dataset to avoid information leakage.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Generic transformation helper"
# Generic transformation helper for MMS metabolite features
transform_features <- function(data,
                               cols,
                               method = c("log1p", "log", "sqrt", "boxcox", 
                                          "inverse_normal", "none"),
                               custom_function = NULL,
                               offset = 1e-6) {
  
  # Check that the selected method is valid
  method <- match.arg(method)
  
  # Select columns using tidyselect syntax
  cols <- tidyselect::eval_select(
    rlang::expr(c({{ cols }})),
    data = data
  )
  cols <- names(cols)
  
  # Return unchanged data if no columns are selected or no transformation is requested
  if (length(cols) == 0 || method == "none") {
    return(data)
  }
  
  # Inverse normal transformation
  inverse_normal_transform <- function(x) {
    r <- rank(x, na.last = "keep", ties.method = "average")
    n <- sum(!is.na(x))
    stats::qnorm((r - 0.5) / n)
  }
  
  # Box-Cox transformation
  boxcox_transform <- function(x) {
    # Box-Cox requires strictly positive values
    min_x <- min(x, na.rm = TRUE)
    
    if (min_x <= 0) {
      x <- x + abs(min_x) + offset
    }
    
    # Estimate lambda by maximum likelihood
    lambda <- stats::optimize(
      f = function(lambda) {
        if (abs(lambda) < 1e-8) {
          xt <- log(x)
        } else {
          xt <- (x^lambda - 1) / lambda
        }
        
        -sum(
          stats::dnorm(
            xt,
            mean = mean(xt, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd = stats::sd(xt, na.rm = TRUE),
            log = TRUE
          ),
          na.rm = TRUE
        )
      },
      interval = c(-2, 2)
    )$minimum
    
    if (abs(lambda) < 1e-8) {
      log(x)
    } else {
      (x^lambda - 1) / lambda
    }
  }
  
  # Apply selected transformation to each selected feature
  for (nm in cols) {
    x <- data[[nm]]
    
    if (!is.null(custom_function)) {
      data[[nm]] <- custom_function(x)
      
    } else if (method == "log1p") {
      data[[nm]] <- log1p(x)
      
    } else if (method == "log") {
      data[[nm]] <- log(x + offset)
      
    } else if (method == "sqrt") {
      data[[nm]] <- sqrt(x)
      
    } else if (method == "inverse_normal") {
      data[[nm]] <- inverse_normal_transform(x)
      
    } else if (method == "boxcox") {
      data[[nm]] <- boxcox_transform(x)
    }
  }
  
  data
}
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Transformation in train and test data"
train_data <- train_data %>%
  transform_features(
    cols = all_of(feature_cols),
    method = "log1p"
  )

test_data <- test_data %>%
  transform_features(
    cols = all_of(feature_cols),
    method = "log1p"
  )
```
:::

**Normalization**

In MMS development, normalization is used to make metabolite predictors more comparable before model training. Whether this step is needed depends on the metabolomics platform and on the preprocessing already performed upstream. In some datasets, major technical normalization has already been completed before analysis, so the main remaining step for MMS construction is to standardize features for modelling.

Within a supervised MMS workflow, normalization should be defined using the training dataset and then applied unchanged to the testing dataset. This helps avoid information leakage and ensures that predictors are represented on the same scale in both subsets. In practice, this is particularly important for penalized regression and other machine-learning models, where differences in metabolite scale can strongly influence model fitting.

In the example workflow, normalization is performed after imputation and log transformation so that metabolite values are complete and less skewed before standardization. When using a Recipes pipeline, this can be implemented with step_normalize(), which estimates normalization parameters in the training data and applies them consistently to new data.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Generic normalization helper"
normalize <- function(data, cols, reference_data = data) {
  cols <- tidyselect::eval_select(rlang::expr(c({{ cols }})), data = data)
  cols <- names(cols)

  if (length(cols) == 0) {
    return(data)
  }

  means <- sapply(reference_data[cols], function(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))
  sds <- sapply(reference_data[cols], function(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))

  # avoid division by zero
  sds[sds == 0 | is.na(sds)] <- 1

  for (nm in cols) {
    data[[nm]] <- (data[[nm]] - means[[nm]]) / sds[[nm]]
  }

  data
}
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Normalization in train and test data"
train_data <- train_data %>%
  normalize(cols = all_of(feature_cols))

test_data <- test_data %>%
  normalize(cols = all_of(feature_cols), reference_data = train_data)
```
:::

**Batch correction** may be needed in MMS workflows when technical batch effects are present, but its use depends on the correction method and on whether it can be applied without compromising the training and testing framework. Because some approaches are not straightforward in prediction settings, batch correction should be used only when technically justified and carefully aligned with the validation design.

**Feature selection** can also be considered before MMS modelling, particularly when the number of metabolites is very large, as it can reduce dimensionality, improve computational efficiency, and remove uninformative variables. At the same time, excluding metabolites too aggressively may weaken the predictive performance of the MMS, especially when the signature depends on many correlated metabolites that each contribute only a small amount of information. In practice, feature selection is more defensible when the aim is to improve interpretability or remove clear noise, whereas for purely predictive MMS construction, methods such as ridge regression are often preferred because they retain the full metabolite set while shrinking coefficients to limit overfitting.

# Building the MMS {#building-the-mms}

This section describes the core supervised MMS workflow. The aim is to train a model that predicts a target exposure from a panel of metabolite features and then use the model-predicted value as the participant-level multimetabolite signature. In this example, the target exposure may first be residualized against selected covariates, the MMS model is trained in the training dataset, and the resulting score is generated in the testing dataset or in another downstream analysis dataset.

**Reusable helper functions:** The helper functions can live in a separate `R/` script, but they can also be documented directly in the Quarto workflow so the full MMS pipeline is visible in one place. The helpers below are designed to keep the workflow modular: define features, residualize exposures if needed, train penalized models, generate MMS scores, standardize them using a reference dataset, and extract coefficients for interpretation.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Reusable helper function"

# Define metabolite feature columns safely.
# Prefer explicit feature names over start_col:ncol(data) whenever possible.
get_feature_columns <- function(data, feature_prefix = NULL, feature_cols = NULL) {
  if (!is.null(feature_cols)) {
    missing_cols <- setdiff(feature_cols, names(data))
    if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
      stop("Some feature columns are missing from data: ",
           paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "))
    }
    return(feature_cols)
  }

  if (!is.null(feature_prefix)) {
    feature_cols <- grep(feature_prefix, names(data), value = TRUE)
    if (length(feature_cols) == 0) {
      stop("No feature columns matched the supplied feature_prefix.")
    }
    return(feature_cols)
  }

  stop("Provide either feature_cols or feature_prefix.")
}


# Residualize one exposure against selected covariates.
# The model should be fitted in the training data only.
residualize_exposure <- function(train_data,
                                 new_data = NULL,
                                 exposure,
                                 covariates,
                                 suffix = "_residual") {
  rhs <- paste(covariates, collapse = " + ")
  formula_obj <- stats::as.formula(paste(exposure, "~", rhs))

  residual_model <- stats::lm(formula_obj, data = train_data)

  residual_name <- paste0(exposure, suffix)

  train_out <- train_data %>%
    dplyr::mutate("{residual_name}" := stats::residuals(residual_model))

  if (is.null(new_data)) {
    return(list(
      train_data = train_out,
      model = residual_model,
      residual_name = residual_name
    ))
  }

  # Residuals in new data are observed values minus expected values
  # based on the model fitted in the training data.
  new_out <- new_data %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      "{residual_name}" := .data[[exposure]] -
        stats::predict(residual_model, newdata = new_data)
    )

  list(
    train_data = train_out,
    new_data = new_out,
    model = residual_model,
    residual_name = residual_name
  )
}


# Fit a single-metabolite screening model for each feature.
# This can be used as an exploratory step, but it is not required before ridge MMS.
single_metabolite_screen <- function(data,
                                     exposure_feature,
                                     feature_cols,
                                     covariates = NULL,
                                     correction = "BH") {
  terms <- c(exposure_feature, covariates)

  results <- purrr::map_dfr(feature_cols, function(feature) {
    model_formula <- stats::reformulate(terms, response = feature)

    stats::lm(model_formula, data = data) %>%
      broom::tidy() %>%
      dplyr::mutate(feature_id = feature, .before = 1)
  })

  results <- results %>%
    dplyr::filter(term == exposure_feature)

  if (!is.null(correction)) {
    results <- results %>%
      dplyr::mutate(p.value_corrected = stats::p.adjust(p.value, method = correction)) %>%
      dplyr::arrange(p.value_corrected)
  } else {
    results <- results %>%
      dplyr::arrange(p.value)
  }

  results
}


# Train one MMS model.
# mixture = 0 gives ridge regression; mixture = 1 gives LASSO;
# values between 0 and 1 give elastic net.
train_mms_model <- function(train_data,
                            exposure_feature,
                            feature_cols,
                            covariates = NULL,
                            mixture = 0,
                            penalty_range = c(-4, 1),
                            penalty_levels = 50,
                            folds = 10,
                            seed = 123,
                            normalize_predictors = TRUE) {
  predictors <- c(covariates, feature_cols)
  model_formula <- stats::reformulate(predictors, response = exposure_feature)

  recipe_obj <- recipes::recipe(model_formula, data = train_data)

  if (normalize_predictors) {
    recipe_obj <- recipe_obj %>%
      recipes::step_normalize(recipes::all_numeric_predictors())
  }

  recipe_obj <- recipe_obj %>%
    recipes::step_dummy(recipes::all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
    recipes::step_zv(recipes::all_predictors())

  model_spec <- parsnip::linear_reg(
    penalty = tune::tune(),
    mixture = mixture
  ) %>%
    parsnip::set_engine("glmnet")

  workflow_obj <- workflows::workflow() %>%
    workflows::add_recipe(recipe_obj) %>%
    workflows::add_model(model_spec)

  set.seed(seed)
  cv_folds <- rsample::vfold_cv(train_data, v = folds)

  tuning_grid <- dials::grid_regular(
    dials::penalty(range = penalty_range),
    levels = penalty_levels
  )

  tuned_results <- tune::tune_grid(
    workflow_obj,
    resamples = cv_folds,
    grid = tuning_grid,
    metrics = yardstick::metric_set(
      yardstick::rmse,
      yardstick::mae,
      yardstick::rsq
    )
  )

  best_params <- tune::select_best(tuned_results, metric = "rmse")
  final_workflow <- tune::finalize_workflow(workflow_obj, best_params)
  final_fit <- generics::fit(final_workflow, data = train_data)

  list(
    final_fit = final_fit,
    cv_results = tuned_results,
    metrics = tune::collect_metrics(tuned_results),
    best_params = best_params,
    folds = cv_folds,
    feature_cols = feature_cols,
    covariates = covariates,
    exposure_feature = exposure_feature,
    mixture = mixture
  )
}


# Generate participant-level MMS scores from a fitted model.
predict_mms_score <- function(model_object, new_data, score_name = "mms_score") {
  score <- stats::predict(model_object$final_fit, new_data = new_data) %>%
    dplyr::pull(.pred)

  new_data %>%
    dplyr::mutate("{score_name}" := score)
}


# Standardize a score using a reference dataset.
# Use the training data as reference when scores must be comparable across datasets.
standardize_from_reference <- function(data,
                                       score_col,
                                       reference_data = data,
                                       new_col = paste0(score_col, "_sd")) {
  score_mean <- mean(reference_data[[score_col]], na.rm = TRUE)
  score_sd <- stats::sd(reference_data[[score_col]], na.rm = TRUE)

  if (is.na(score_sd) || score_sd == 0) {
    stop("The reference standard deviation is zero or missing.")
  }

  data %>%
    dplyr::mutate("{new_col}" := (.data[[score_col]] - score_mean) / score_sd)
}


# Extract glmnet coefficients from a finalized tidymodels workflow.
extract_mms_coefficients <- function(model_object) {
  penalty_value <- model_object$best_params$penalty[[1]]

  workflows::extract_fit_parsnip(model_object$final_fit) %>%
    parsnip::extract_fit_engine() %>%
    stats::coef(s = penalty_value) %>%
    as.matrix() %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("feature_id") %>%
    dplyr::rename(coefficient = 2) %>%
    dplyr::filter(feature_id != "(Intercept)") %>%
    dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(abs(coefficient)))
}
```
:::

## Feature selection or exposure residualization {#feature-selection}

Feature selection is optional and depends on the scientific goal. For ridge regression, all metabolite predictors are retained and coefficients are shrunk, so a separate metabolite-filtering step is usually not required. For LASSO or elastic net, feature selection is part of model fitting because some coefficients may be shrunk to zero.

A common MMS step is not feature selection but **exposure residualization**. This is useful when the target exposure should represent variation independent of total energy intake, correlated dietary components, demographic characteristics, or other predefined covariates. To avoid leakage, residualization should be fitted in the training data and then applied to the testing data using the same residual model.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Feature selection"
#| 
# Example: define metabolite feature columns
feature_columns <- get_feature_columns(
  data = signature_training_df,
  feature_cols = feature_columns
)

# Residualize the exposure using training data only
residualized_exposure_a <- residualize_exposure(
  train_data = signature_training_df,
  new_data = signature_testing_df,
  exposure = "exposure_a",
  covariates = c("total_energy", "age", "sex", "bmi")
)

signature_training_df <- residualized_exposure_a$train_data
signature_testing_df <- residualized_exposure_a$new_data

# Store the residualized exposure name for model training
target_outcomes <- c(
  exposure_a = residualized_exposure_a$residual_name
)

# Optional single-metabolite screening
screening_results <- single_metabolite_screen(
  data = signature_training_df,
  exposure_feature = "exposure_a_residual",
  feature_cols = feature_columns,
  covariates = c("age", "sex", "bmi"),
  correction = "BH"
)
```
:::

## Model training {#model-training}

In MMS development, several penalized regression approaches can be used depending on the goal of the signature. **Ridge regression** uses all available metabolite predictors while shrinking their coefficients, which can be useful when metabolites are highly correlated and the aim is to construct a stable multimetabolite score. **LASSO** encourages sparsity by shrinking some coefficients to zero, making it useful when the goal includes metabolite selection or a more parsimonious signature. **Elastic net** combines ridge and LASSO penalties, allowing correlated metabolites to be partly retained while still performing some variable selection.

The choice between ridge, LASSO, and elastic net is controlled by the mixture parameter, also known as `alpha` in `glmnet`: `alpha = 0` corresponds to ridge regression, `alpha = 1` corresponds to LASSO, and values between 0 and 1 correspond to elastic net models. For any of these approaches, the penalty parameter should be tuned in the training data using cross-validation. The final MMS model is then fitted in the full training dataset using the selected penalty and applied to new data to generate participant-level MMS scores.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Model training"

target_outcomes <- c(
  exposure_a = "exposure_a_residual",
  exposure_b = "exposure_b_residual",
  exposure_c = "exposure_c_residual"
)

# Fit one ridge MMS model per target exposure
signature_models <- purrr::imap(
  target_outcomes,
  ~ train_mms_model(
    train_data = signature_training_df,
    exposure_feature = .x,
    feature_cols = feature_columns,
    covariates = NULL,
    mixture = 0,
    penalty_levels = 50,
    folds = 10,
    seed = 123,
    normalize_predictors = TRUE
  )
)

# Store selected penalties
best_lambdas <- purrr::map_dbl(
  signature_models,
  ~ .x$best_params$penalty[[1]]
)

# Collect cross-validation performance
cv_metric_summary <- purrr::imap_dfr(
  signature_models,
  ~ .x$metrics %>%
    dplyr::mutate(signature = .y, .before = 1)
)
```
:::

## Score construction {#score-construction}

The MMS score is the model-predicted value for each participant. In other words, once the penalized regression model has learned the weighted combination of metabolites that predicts the target exposure, the predicted value from that model becomes the participant-level MMS. The score can be generated in the testing dataset, the full study dataset, or an external validation dataset as long as the same preprocessing and model object are used.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Score construction"
# Generate MMS scores in the testing dataset
signature_testing_results <- signature_testing_df

for (signature_name in names(signature_models)) {
  score_name <- paste0("signature_score_", signature_name)

  signature_testing_results <- predict_mms_score(
    model_object = signature_models[[signature_name]],
    new_data = signature_testing_results,
    score_name = score_name
  )
}

# Generate MMS scores in the full analysis dataset
analysis_with_scores <- analysis_df

for (signature_name in names(signature_models)) {
  score_name <- paste0("signature_score_", signature_name)

  analysis_with_scores <- predict_mms_score(
    model_object = signature_models[[signature_name]],
    new_data = analysis_with_scores,
    score_name = score_name
  )
}
```
:::

## Score standardization {#score-standardization}

MMS scores are often standardized so that downstream estimates are interpreted per one standard deviation of the signature. The reference distribution should be defined clearly. For internal validation, the testing set can be standardized within itself. For transportability or comparison across datasets, it is usually better to standardize using the training-set score distribution and apply the same mean and standard deviation to the testing or downstream dataset.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "MMS score standardization"

# First generate training scores to define the reference distribution
signature_training_results <- signature_training_df

for (signature_name in names(signature_models)) {
  score_name <- paste0("signature_score_", signature_name)

  signature_training_results <- predict_mms_score(
    model_object = signature_models[[signature_name]],
    new_data = signature_training_results,
    score_name = score_name
  )

  signature_testing_results <- standardize_from_reference(
    data = signature_testing_results,
    score_col = score_name,
    reference_data = signature_training_results,
    new_col = paste0(score_name, "_sd")
  )

  analysis_with_scores <- standardize_from_reference(
    data = analysis_with_scores,
    score_col = score_name,
    reference_data = signature_training_results,
    new_col = paste0(score_name, "_sd")
  )
}
```
:::

##  {#lasso-metabolite-selection}

## Weighted metabolite scores {#weighted-metabolite-scores}

The predicted values from the penalized model become the MMS score. These can then be standardized for interpretation per standard deviation.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Weighted metabolite scores"
all_signature_scores <- purrr::imap(
  signature_models,
  ~ predict_train_model(.x, analysis_df)
)

analysis_df <- dplyr::bind_cols(
  analysis_df,
  purrr::set_names(as.data.frame(all_signature_scores), paste0("signature_score_", names(all_signature_scores)))
) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("signature_score_"), scale, .names = "{.col}_sd"))
```
:::

# Model evaluation {#model-evaluation}

Model evaluation asks whether the MMS score reproduces the target exposure in data not used for model training. For continuous exposures, the main validation metrics are usually R\^2, RMSE, MAE, and the slope from regressing the observed or residualized exposure on the MMS score. If the MMS is later evaluated against a binary or time-to-event health outcome, that becomes a downstream epidemiological analysis rather than the primary MMS construction metric.

## R2 {#r2}

`R^2` quantifies the proportion of variation in the target exposure explained by the MMS score in the testing dataset. When both the target exposure and MMS score are standardized, the slope can also be interpreted as the expected SD difference in the target exposure per one SD higher MMS.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "R2 and regression-based validation"

evaluate_mms_regression <- function(data, truth, estimate, signature_name = NULL) {
  eval_df <- data %>%
    dplyr::select(
      truth = dplyr::all_of(truth),
      estimate = dplyr::all_of(estimate)
    ) %>%
    tidyr::drop_na()

  fit <- stats::lm(truth ~ estimate, data = eval_df)

  slope <- broom::tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
    dplyr::filter(term == "estimate")

  fit_summary <- broom::glance(fit)

  tibble::tibble(
    signature = signature_name,
    n = nrow(eval_df),
    beta = slope$estimate,
    conf.low = slope$conf.low,
    conf.high = slope$conf.high,
    p.value = slope$p.value,
    r_squared = fit_summary$r.squared,
    adj_r_squared = fit_summary$adj.r.squared
  )
}

evaluation_specs <- list(
  exposure_a = list(
    truth = "exposure_a_residual",
    estimate = "signature_score_exposure_a"
  ),
  exposure_b = list(
    truth = "exposure_b_residual",
    estimate = "signature_score_exposure_b"
  )
)

evaluation_results <- purrr::imap_dfr(
  evaluation_specs,
  ~ evaluate_mms_regression(
    data = signature_testing_results,
    truth = .x$truth,
    estimate = .x$estimate,
    signature_name = .y
  )
)
```
:::

## RMSE and MAE {#rmse}

RMSE and MAE summarize prediction error. RMSE penalizes larger errors more strongly, while MAE is easier to interpret as the average absolute difference between the observed exposure and the MMS-predicted exposure. These metrics are most interpretable when the target and score are on the same scale.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Prediction error metrics"

evaluate_mms_error <- function(data, truth, estimate, signature_name = NULL) {
  eval_df <- data %>%
    dplyr::select(
      truth = dplyr::all_of(truth),
      estimate = dplyr::all_of(estimate)
    ) %>%
    tidyr::drop_na()

  tibble::tibble(
    signature = signature_name,
    n = nrow(eval_df),
    rmse = yardstick::rmse_vec(
      truth = eval_df$truth,
      estimate = eval_df$estimate
    ),
    mae = yardstick::mae_vec(
      truth = eval_df$truth,
      estimate = eval_df$estimate
    ),
    rsq = yardstick::rsq_vec(
      truth = eval_df$truth,
      estimate = eval_df$estimate
    )
  )
}

prediction_error_results <- purrr::imap_dfr(
  evaluation_specs,
  ~ evaluate_mms_error(
    data = signature_testing_results,
    truth = .x$truth,
    estimate = .x$estimate,
    signature_name = .y
  )
)
```
:::

## ROC / AUC {#roc-auc}

ROC curves and AUC are useful only when the MMS is evaluated against a binary outcome, such as case-control status. This is different from evaluating how well the MMS predicts the original continuous exposure. In this setting, the MMS is treated as an epidemiological predictor or biomarker, and the AUC quantifies discrimination between outcome groups.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "ROC / AUC for downstream binary outcomes"

evaluate_binary_outcome_auc <- function(data, outcome, score, event_level = "second") {
  data %>%
    dplyr::select(
      outcome = dplyr::all_of(outcome),
      score = dplyr::all_of(score)
    ) %>%
    tidyr::drop_na() %>%
    yardstick::roc_auc(
      truth = outcome,
      score,
      event_level = event_level
    )
}

roc_auc_result <- evaluate_binary_outcome_auc(
  data = downstream_analysis_df,
  outcome = "outcome_case_status",
  score = "signature_score_exposure_a_sd"
)
```
:::



## Cross-validation results {#cross-validation-results}

Cross-validation outputs can be summarized by storing fold-specific coefficients and then computing medians and interquartile ranges.

If you prefer a more abstract interface, the cross-validation helpers above can be used as a lightweight wrapper pair for repeated cross-validated training and testing.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Cross-validation results"
summarize_cv_coefficients <- function(model_object, feature_annotation_df = NULL) {
  recipe_obj <- workflows::extract_recipe(model_object$final_fit)
  penalty_value <- model_object$best_params$penalty[[1]]
  mixture_value <- model_object$best_params$mixture[[1]]
  exposure_feature <- model_object$exposure_feature

  fold_coefficients <- purrr::map(model_object$folds$splits, function(split) {
    fold_training_df <- rsample::analysis(split)
    prepped_recipe <- recipes::prep(recipe_obj, training = fold_training_df, retain = TRUE)
    baked_fold <- recipes::juice(prepped_recipe)

    x_fold <- baked_fold %>%
      dplyr::select(-dplyr::all_of(exposure_feature)) %>%
      as.matrix()

    y_fold <- baked_fold[[exposure_feature]]

    glmnet::glmnet(
      x = x_fold,
      y = y_fold,
      alpha = mixture_value,
      lambda = penalty_value
    ) %>%
      coef() %>%
      as.matrix()
  })

  coefficient_df <- do.call(cbind, fold_coefficients)
  coefficient_df <- coefficient_df[rownames(coefficient_df) %in% model_object$metabolite_columns, , drop = FALSE]

  coefficient_summary <- as.data.frame(coefficient_df) %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("feature_id") %>%
    mutate(
      median = apply(dplyr::pick(-feature_id), 1, quantile, probs = 0.5),
      q1 = apply(dplyr::pick(-feature_id), 1, quantile, probs = 0.25),
      q3 = apply(dplyr::pick(-feature_id), 1, quantile, probs = 0.75)
    )

  if (!is.null(feature_annotation_df)) {
    coefficient_summary <- coefficient_summary %>%
      left_join(feature_annotation_df, by = "feature_id")
  }

  coefficient_summary
}

coefficient_summary_list <- purrr::map(
  signature_models,
  ~ summarize_cv_coefficients(.x, feature_annotation_df = feature_annotation_df)
)
```
:::

# Robustness and reproducibility {#robustness-and-reproducibility}

Once the MMS scores are created, they can be carried into downstream epidemiological models and sensitivity analyses.

## Sensitivity analyses {#sensitivity-analyses}

The original project tested whether MMS-outcome associations were robust to alternative adjustment sets and interaction terms. A generic version is shown below for conditional logistic regression, but the same principle applies to other models.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Sensitivity analyses"
downstream_model_formulas <- list(
  "Base-adjusted" = ~ covariate_1 + covariate_2 + strata(matching_set_id),
  "Fully-adjusted" = ~ covariate_1 + covariate_2 + covariate_3 + covariate_4 + strata(matching_set_id),
  "Sensitivity-adjusted" = ~ covariate_1 + covariate_2 + covariate_3 + covariate_4 + sensitivity_covariate + strata(matching_set_id)
)

fit_conditional_model <- function(data, signature_name, model_label, rhs_formula) {
  predictor_name <- paste0("signature_score_", signature_name, "_sd")
  rhs_string <- as.character(rhs_formula)[2]
  full_formula <- as.formula(paste0("binary_outcome ~ ", predictor_name, " + ", rhs_string))

  survival::clogit(full_formula, data = data, method = "efron", robust = TRUE) %>%
    broom::tidy(conf.int = TRUE) %>%
    dplyr::filter(term == predictor_name)
}
```
:::

This is the point in the workflow where the MMS score leaves the pure prediction setting and becomes an epidemiological exposure variable for downstream association models.

## Stability of metabolite selection {#stability-of-metabolite-selection}

Coefficient stability across cross-validation folds helps identify which metabolites consistently contribute to the signature.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Stability of metabolite selection"
top_features_table <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  lapply(names(coefficient_summary_list), function(signature_name) {
    coefficient_summary_list[[signature_name]] %>%
      mutate(signature = signature_name)
  })
) %>%
  group_by(signature) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(median)), .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 30)
```
:::

## Reproducibility across folds {#reproducibility-across-folds}

For transparent reporting, it is useful to export coefficient summaries, downstream association tables, and figures derived from the same standardized workflow.

::: {.callout-note .callout-code-example}
## Example code

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#| code-summary: "Reproducibility across folds"
readr::write_csv(top_features_table, "results/signature_top_features.csv")
readr::write_csv(evaluation_results, "results/signature_evaluation_results.csv")
```
:::

This generic structure can be adapted to:

-   dietary exposures
-   clinical biomarkers
-   disease risk signatures
-   survival outcomes
-   interaction and subgroup analyses

The key idea is to keep the workflow modular: preprocess, split data, fit the MMS, validate the score, and then carry the standardized score into downstream epidemiological models.

Some reusable helper patterns that fit naturally into this workflow are:

-   simulation helpers for teaching and examples
-   preprocessing wrappers
-   train/test splitting helpers
-   single-metabolite screening helpers
-   model-training helpers for elastic net, random forest, and k-nearest neighbors
-   score-calculation helpers
-   regression and classification testing helpers
